exact_spoken_take_hits.transcript:
I apologized.

Sella wanted to know what I needed.

Several answers arrived at once.

Proof that time had moved backward.

An explanation for why my mana barely answered.

A list of people I remembered losing.

Training.

Money.

A better sword.

Someone to tell me I was not losing my mind.

Too much.

I put the Bronze token on the counter instead and asked what it currently got me.

That word caught her.

Currently.

She turned the token over and gave me the list.

Basic yard access. Contract board. Guild beds if available. Discounted healer. One assessment each quarter.

Apparently I had missed my last one.

Probably.

Training yard included. Instructors not included.

Rates were posted on the board three feet to my right.

I had walked past it.

Of course I had.

I read the prices.

Then read them again.

Obscene.

One silver for instruction.

Yes.

Exactly.

Sella looked at my coat.

Then my sword.

Then me.

Something happened behind her eyes.

Three copper.

She had somehow landed on three copper.

I stared at her.

Why three?

"You have the face."

There.

Apparently I had spent fifty-nine years acquiring expertise and several expressions everybody else had been cataloguing without permission.

I told her I had enough.

Three copper.

Enough for the yard.

Which was free.

Exactly.

She gave the token back and ended the conversation by looking past me.

Next.

I stayed.

My free hour was over.

I had accomplished less than I expected and learned more than I wanted.

At the desk, Sella held out her hand.

Token.

I gave it to her.

She stamped the register and informed me the next free yard block was in six days.

Six.

Bronze basic access.

I needed daily.

"Then pay."

There it was.

Short enough that there was nowhere for me to hide from it.

One silver for instruction. Copper for additional yard blocks. More for practice gear if I broke anything. More for healer access. More for food if I wanted the body to recover properly.

Mana conditioning would cost too, once I found someone willing to teach a nineteen-year-old whose mana currently answered like a sleepy cat.

I had three copper this morning.

Two now, after breakfast.

Cheaper yard?

Outside.

Posts?

Trees.

Level ground?

Mostly.

Would anyone complain if I hit them?

Sella looked at me.

The trees, probably not.

People depended on my accuracy.

That was almost a joke.

Future Sella existed in there somewhere.

Present Sella had already reached for the next form.

Conversation over.

Fine.

I left.

Future knowledge was much easier to spend before I tried to buy anything with it.

The east market gave me three possibilities in the first hour.

One was wrong.

One was real but useless for another twenty years.

The third was a pile of gray stone chips beside a masonry stall.

Kestrin shale.

I stopped.

Cheap. Brittle. Mildly mana-reactive. Mostly used where nobody cared if it cracked.

Later, it mattered.

I knew that.

Probably.

There was that word again.

I remembered pale filtration housings stamped with the Arwick mark. Old Kestrin waste binding alchemical residue under heat. Finished filters cheap enough that nobody important bothered to think about them.

That was all.

No formula. No inventor. No exact year.

I had the ending of a story and none of the useful middle.

Still better than two copper.

The stall owner wanted two silver for the cart.

I had two copper.

Right.

A bucket was one copper.

I bought the bucket.

Growth.

The old me would have bought the cart because scale felt like confidence.

Current me had just been hit in the ribs by Jorren and nearly walked into vegetables while practicing footwork.

A bucket was enough to be wrong with.

I asked whether he worked with mana-reactive ceramic mixes.

Sometimes.

Powdered Kestrin in a porous body?

“Why would I?”

There it was.

The dangerous moment.

My memory wanted to become authority because I knew the finished world.

I made myself stay with what I actually had.

“Trace mana. Cheap structure. High surface area if powdered. I think heat changes how it binds residue.”

He looked at the bucket again.

“Think?”

“Yes.”

“Based on?”

Something I had seen a long time ago.

He looked at my face.

“You're nineteen.”

Right.

“It was a very formative childhood.”

Nothing.

No laugh.

I liked him more.

His name was Arlo.

Good.

Not proof.

But good.

“Arlo Arwick?”

He went still.

Ah.

Mistake.

“Who told you my family name?”

No sign on the door.

No maker's stamp visible from where I stood.

Excellent work, Greg.

I blamed the cooper.

Arlo told me the cooper didn't know his family name.

Of course he didn't.

I looked at the lamp regulator.

Could he test the shale?

His expression said the subject had not changed.

Mine said I hoped persistence counted as strategy.

Arlo finally took one chip from the bucket.

Turned it over.

“Six silver.”

I laughed.

He put it back.

“Then no.”

For a test?

“For my time. Materials extra.”

Right.

Six silver for his time.

I called it robbery.

He suggested a cheaper artificer.

I did not know a cheaper artificer.

Worse, I did not know whether the Arwick name mattered because of Arlo, his children, a buyer who kept the name, or a coincidence large enough to make me look stupid.

Future knowledge had given me a door.

The door charged six silver.

I took the bucket outside and sat on the cooper's back step.

Two copper.

Training would cost.

The test cost six silver before materials.

Food mattered if I intended to train every day.

Mana conditioning would cost once I found a teacher.

Rent would eventually become interested in me.

My second life had lasted less than two days and already required financing.

That part felt familiar.

There were several lenders in Carrow.

I knew one.

That was not the same thing as trusting him.

A month later, Sella stopped asking for my guild token.

That was how I noticed the month.

Not the calendar. Not the tally marks beside my bed. Not the increasingly complicated page where I had attempted to track training, debt, food, mana, shale, and several financial decisions that became less defensible when arranged chronologically.

Sella looked up when I entered, reached beneath the counter, and slid the yard register toward me before I had finished reaching for the token.

Habit.

Mine and hers.

That was time.

Jorren was leaning against the end of the counter in new boots.

That was time too.

I noticed the boots because the old pair had split along the inside heel three weeks ago and he had complained about the repair cost for most of a sparring session.

"You got the escort."

He looked down.

"You remember that?"

I had forgotten his name twice during our first week.

Apparently my memory had priorities.

The north-road caravan left in nine days.

Jorren had spent the month earning enough contract credit to get taken on. He had done this while I was busy proving that future knowledge became substantially less impressive when converted into rent, training fees, experimental ceramics, loan interest, and food.

His life had moved without me.

Good.

Annoying, somehow, but good.

Sella tapped the register.

I signed.

My handwriting had gotten worse.

The hard patch under my first finger had gotten better.

I flexed the hand once after putting the pen down.

Jorren noticed.

"Training?"

Everything, really.

The first week had mostly improved my appetite. The second changed my feet. By the third, the overhead cut had stopped feeling like a set of instructions I was delivering to my own joints.

It was not excellent.

It was not Silver.

It was definitely not some hidden S-class inheritance waiting for nineteen-year-old muscles to remember greatness.

It was mine.

That mattered more.

The Guild board mattered more immediately.

One contract had been circled twice in Sella's handwriting.

Old bathhouse near the south wall. Two saltbacks confirmed. Possible third. Acid hazard. Five silver plus salvage.

The listing had been there six days.

Five silver was enough to become attractive around day four.

Vale currently owned part of my week.

Arlo currently owned most of the money I had not given Vale.

The shale experiment had produced one repeatable improvement and several expensive ways to make ugly ceramic.

My mana had improved from almost nothing to a small stable pulse I could hold for several breaths.

That had also developed a price.

Everything useful had.

I took the contract off the board.

“Why did the new mix work?”

Arlo corrected the question.

It had worked better.

Not worked.

Better.

Right.

That distinction mattered.

He had changed the clay body first, then the firing schedule. He thought flow mattered more than the mana reaction I had originally obsessed over.

I thought surface area still mattered.

He agreed that it probably did.

Probably.

There was that word again.

My favorite word.

The difference was that Arlo now had measurements attached to his probably.

I had a memory of an object that did not exist yet.

I was beginning to understand why this arrangement irritated both of us.

And why it might work.

The problem was that we did not actually have an arrangement.

Right.

That part had been waiting for us.

It became obvious when I asked what he wanted to do with the six disks.

Arlo went still in a different way than he had when I accidentally used his family name.

Not suspicion.

Preparation.

He had been waiting for this.

The disk split.

Concentrated wash went over the side.

Then something in the waste started reacting near the hot line.

I looked back at the crack.

"Reacting how?"

Ivena's eyes narrowed.

"Come look."

Good answer.

We went.

Mill Street smelled better from a distance.

Up close it was wet wool, hot metal, ash, mordant, soap, old water, and enough competing dye to make the air feel colored.

Ivena's shop occupied the ground floor of a long narrow building with vents cut high into the walls. Three large vats sat along one side. Copper troughs carried wash toward a stone drain channel in the floor. Racks of cloth hung overhead in strips of red, green, yellow, and several shades of purple I would previously have described as purple.

Apparently this was wrong.

Ivena had names for all of them.

She used three while pointing out exactly what our disk had ruined.

I remembered none.

The important part was the equipment.

Arlo's workshop tests had used bowls.

Small pour.

Cool enough to hold.

One pass at a time.

Ivena's line used a raised copper reservoir feeding a narrow housing beside the second vat. Warm wash ran through it for long stretches. Not boiling. Hot enough that the copper stayed warm after the flow stopped.

Different volume.

Different duration.

Different temperature.

Different problem.

The housing itself had been wiped clean, but the floor beneath it had not.

Purple stain ran toward the drain in a wide fan.

At the center, the color was nearly black.

One copper fitting above it had a strange pale mark crawling around the edge.

Not corrosion.

I crouched.

The hair on my forearm lifted.

Mana.

Very little.

Enough.

Ivena saw me notice.

"That."

Arlo crouched beside me.

He touched the dry stone near the stain, then stopped before touching the dark center.

Good.

"What is in the wash?"

Ivena listed things I mostly understood.

Pigment. Binding salt. Ash treatment. A cheap mana-set additive used to keep the darker purple from washing gray.

There.

Mana-set additive.

How much?

Not much.

Usually.

I looked at the stain again.

Usually did not matter if the filter was concentrating it.

Arlo heard the same thought in a different language.

"The disk was catching more than the sludge."

Maybe.

Ivena folded her arms.

"Is that bad?"

We did not know yet.

Her expression explained that this answer had limited commercial value.

Fair.

Arlo wanted to see the housing.

Ivena wanted to know whether opening it would make the floor do that again.

Also fair.

We compromised by being careful, which is the traditional stage before discovering how careful was insufficient.

The feed valve was closed.

The reservoir was mostly empty.

The line had cooled.

Arlo loosened the housing bolts one at a time.

I stood to the side instead of directly in front of it.

Current life had improved me.

A little.

The last bolt came loose.

Nothing happened.

Good.

Arlo pulled the housing apart.

The remaining piece of disk came with it.

Purple-black paste filled the ceramic pores along one side.

Not evenly.

The lower half was packed.

Upper half much less.

Flow problem.

Ivena pointed.

"That's where it slowed."

Arlo did not answer.

He had gone very still.

I knew that stillness now.

His version of shouting.

He scraped a tiny amount of the paste onto a metal pick.

The pick warmed in his fingers.

He dropped it.

It hit the wet stone.

Purple light moved across the water.

Not bright.

Fast.

A thin crawling line ran toward the copper trough.

Every later-life instinct I had woke up at once.

Not memories exactly.

Shape.

Failure shape.

Conductive path.

Wet floor.

Metal.

Mana-bearing residue.

People standing inside it.

"Back."

Ivena moved immediately.

Good.

Arlo did not.

He was staring at the pick.

I grabbed the back of his coat and pulled.

The purple line touched the trough.

Copper rang.

One clean note.

Then the entire wet section of trough flashed violet along the seam.

A worker at the far vat turned toward us.

Too close.

"Off the floor."

He froze.

Wrong response.

I pointed at the dry platform beside him.

"Up. Now."

That worked.

He climbed.

The line of light continued along the copper toward the raised reservoir.

I knew what I would have done forty years later.

Barrier under the seam.

Cut the conductive path.

Contain the spill.

Buy everyone ten seconds.

Simple.

I put out my hand.

Reached for mana.

The remembered motion was enormous.

The answer was not.

Pressure behind my eyes.

A weak pulse down my arm.

Then pain.

No barrier.

Not even close.

For one ugly second I was fifty-nine again in my head and nineteen everywhere that mattered.

The copper rang a second time.

Reality did not care.

Fine.

No barrier.

What did I have?

People.

Valves.

Dry wood.

Ash bins.

Drain channel.

A ceramic lid leaning against the wall.

Stupid.

Instinct.

Mana answered this time.

Not a wall.

Not even a proper barrier.

A palm-wide shimmer snapped into existence in front of my hand.

Thin.

Crooked.

Beautiful.

The stream hit it.

For less than a second, the liquid split around my palm instead of through it.

Then the shimmer vanished.

The rest struck the ceramic lid.

I turned my face away.

Hot droplets hit my sleeve.

Not acid.

Still unpleasant.

Arlo stumbled back onto dry stone.

The pipe stopped knocking.

The violet line faded along the trough.

Silence.

Not complete silence.

Dyehouse silence.

Water dripping.

Somebody breathing too loudly.

A vat bubbling because nobody had told the other two vats that the scene was over.

I looked at my hand.

Nothing there.

No barrier.

Of course not.

But it had been there.

One breath.

Less.

Enough to change where the first part of the spray went.

My arm started shaking.

I lowered it before anyone could mistake that for drama.

Ivena walked over.

Flow rate?

Higher for the same reason.

How long before slowing?

Longer than the first two full tests combined.

Arlo's face changed.

He was no longer defending the disk.

He was collecting the failure.

Good.

Ivena knew her process.

Arlo knew the material.

I knew enough about later systems to recognize that neither of those jobs belonged to me.

My job was somewhere else.

Connections.

What changed?

What became dangerous?

What mattered next?

Heat.

Flow.

Time under load.

Concentration.

Maybe mana salt.

Maybe all of them.

A month ago I would have tried to solve all five before leaving the building.

Current me had recently been introduced to ceilings.

I picked two.

Arlo needed to reproduce the clog under warm continuous flow.

Ivena needed a way to bypass the disk before pressure built if the flow slowed again.

Everything else could wait until those answers existed.

Arlo looked at me.

That was almost approval.

Ivena wanted the fitting checked first.

Correct.

Her shop.

Her order.

We paid her.

Mostly Arlo.

I had just paid Vale and was once again rich primarily in arguments.

And a bypass.

He nodded.

The dyer had become part of the experiment whether either of us liked it or not.

Also good.

I sat on the repaired stool and looked at my hand again.

One pulse.

One crooked shimmer.

Enough to move liquid for less than a second.

My sword had taken a month to become mine.

Maybe mana would take longer.

Maybe much longer.

That hurt more than the sword had.

Swordsmanship was something I had respected.

Support was what I had become.

There are failures that tell you what you cannot do.

This one had done something worse.

It reminded me what I wanted back.

Outside, someone rolled a cart through the alley.

The wheel hit a stone and rattled.

Arlo started measuring clay.

I had almost no money.

Jorren left north soon.

Our first customer wanted a refund, a repair, and possibly another filter.

My old magic existed in my body as approximately one badly shaped breath.

Progress.

Apparently.

Under where the stone would swing if the bracket let go.

I ran.

No mana.

Did not even reach for it.

There was no four-inch solution to several hundred pounds of limestone.

One child saw me coming and froze.

The mother turned.

Wrong direction.

"Wall!"

She looked at the wall.

Good enough.

I grabbed the older child by the shoulder and shoved him toward the west pier. The mother followed because children remained a better command system than strangers.
